subject: treasureHoard
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: treasure hoard: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a treasure hoard prop module in League of Legends style—coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets, all gold with a teal magic glow—and thinking through the required single root joint structure even though this is a static prop group rather than a creature.

I'm sketching the dimensions for the chest and the mound of coins, plus a hinged lid joint so it can open, while settling on which builder APIs (part, extrude, lathe, sweep, rod, spike, glow kit) I trust enough to use safely without testing. Now I'm working out the color palette: a dark blue-purple chest with gold trim and hextech-style glow, ruby/sapphire/emerald/amethyst gems, and a lathe-turned gold crown.

I'm figuring out the joint hierarchy next, placing the root at the origin and a hinge joint at the back of the lid, then working through the rotation math to make sure opening the lid tips its front edge upward about the x-axis without the lid clipping through the chest when open.

I'll build the lid parts in their closed position and apply the opening pose afterward, since later parts inherit the new pose. I'm now settling on an opening angle around -100° and sketching out the chest's width and depth dimensions to make sure the open lid fits properly and treasure can spill visibly from the opening.

I'm figuring out the lid shape as a half-cylinder extruded along the chest's width, working out the axis orientation and profile so the barrel curve sits correctly relative to the hinge.

I'll squash the arc slightly with Rz=0.3, Ry=0.2 and add a small bevel, then set up the hinge joint at the back-bottom of the lid so it rotates roughly -105° about that point, swinging the front up and standing the lid behind.

For the main body, I'm building a box shape with painted wood textures and grain, considering a Hextech-style palette—maybe a deep indigo or navy wood tone with gold trim accents for contrast.

Adding plank seam lines and a subtle lighting effect, with a custom paint function that layers horizontal plank divisions over the base wood grain, then applies a warm-top/cool-bottom lighting tint by resolving the underlying color at each point.

For the chest geometry, I'm reconsidering the open-lid structure — rather than a solid box, I want actual wall panels with an inner floor so the hollow interior is visible, filled with a gold coin mound rising up near the rim.

I'll add a thin red velvet lining just inside the wood walls, offset slightly, to give the inside a visible fabric texture beneath the gold.

Now I'm working out the gold corner straps wrapping the chest body — thin box plates positioned at the front, sides, and corners to mimic banded reinforcement over the wood.

I'll simplify and just use individual rivet parts rather than merging geometry, since the count is small enough to stay under the limit. For the lock, I'm planning a gold shield texture with a keyhole and gem on a plane, placed as a hasp plate on the lid's front edge where it hangs once the lid is open.

Checking the lid's curved front geometry, I realize the front face has a vertical tangent, so I'll instead mount the keyhole plate on the body's front center and add a small gold hasp tongue box on the lid's front bottom edge. For the lid bands, I'm adding thin arched straps along the sides using a slightly larger profile extruded along the x-axis.

I'm nudging the band's bottom edge down slightly to avoid z-fighting with the lid's underside where their flat faces would otherwise overlap, since this won't be visible when the lid is closed anyway.

When the lid is open, that flat bottom face becomes visible facing the viewer, so I want to add an interior lining there — a thin red plate offset slightly outward from the lid surface, possibly with a gold crest decal oriented to face downward.

For the coins, my plan is to build a lumpy gold dome mound as the base shape, then scatter individual coin cylinders across its surface using random sampling, orienting each coin along the surface normal with some tilt and spin variation so it looks like a natural pile spilling out of the chest.

I'm placing the main mound inside the chest cavity and adding a second flattened overflow pile in front near the rim, letting the lowest points sink slightly into the floor for a settled look.

Realizing bounding boxes would reveal negative y if the spheres sink below the floor, I switch to hemisphere geometries (sphere with thetaLength capped at π/2) for the piles so the flat side rests exactly at y=0, avoiding any visible clipping while keeping the rounded dune shape on top. For scattering coins across these mound surfaces, I plan to filter by surface normal so only upward-facing areas (n.y > 0.2) get coins, skipping hidden undersides.

For coin counts, I estimate around 150 coins across the piles, each a separate low-poly cylinder (~40 triangles), keeping total triangle and part counts well within budget even alongside other scene elements. For texturing, I'm wary that mapping a circular emblem texture onto a cylinder will create an ugly vertical strip on the side faces, so I need the texture to read as solid gold rather than show a stretched stripe pattern there.

Instead I'll design a grayscale coin texture (opaque light background, darker rim and crown emblem) that gets tinted by the part's gold color, letting me reuse one texture across a few gold variants as separate tinted materials. I'm mapping the cylinder's cap UVs using standard circular projection, and for variety I'll have a few coins standing upright and partially buried in the pile rather than all lying flat.

For gems, I'm considering faceted geometries like octahedron or icosahedron, or a custom lathed gem profile with a pointed bottom and faceted crown, flat-shaded for a jewel look. I want some gems to glow using bright jewel-tone colors (ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, hextech cyan), with a few larger hexagonal crystal shards standing taller for visual variety.

For the crown, I'm placing it tilted on top of one of the piles, built from a hollow lathed circlet band with spiky fleur-shaped points extruded around the ring, each spike capped with a tiny gem.

Still designing crown details...

Setting up coordinate transform helpers...

I'm uncertain whether region.part bakes scale into orientation correctly, so I'll avoid that risk and instead use region.p and region.d directly for positions and directions, calling b.part myself with those raw values.

For bone assignment, I need to figure out which bone each part snaps to by default—since geometry attaches to whichever bone passes closest, and the root joint's children determine that mapping.

Since parts located near the lid joint could accidentally get assigned to the lid's bone and rotate with it unintentionally, I'll explicitly pass `bone: root` for all parts that shouldn't move with the lid, using a helper function to apply that consistently.

For the goblets, I'm planning lathe profiles with a foot, stem, and bowl, using gold material with gem accents on the bowl, and thinking through the axis outline needed to shape it correctly.

Still plotting the goblet outline coordinates...

I'm planning to differentiate the three goblets visually: one filled with coins and gems, one glowing with red wine, and one tipped over and spilled.

For the tipped goblet, I need to tilt the lathe axis rather than keep it vertical, so I'm working out an angled axis direction and making sure its lowest point stays above the ground plane, accounting for the overall model height with the chest and open lid.

For a goblet lying on its side, I need to tilt the axis so the lowest point stays above ground, accounting for the bowl radius being larger than the foot radius—so the foot end lifts slightly while the bowl end sits lower.

Choosing a tilt angle of about 4.6 degrees so the bowl clears the floor while resting on its foot rim and bowl edge. For the goblet lying at the front-left, I'm defining its origin and axis direction, then scattering coins near the mouth opening outward along that axis to simulate them spilling out.

Those spilled coins lie flat near the floor, with their thin cylindrical thickness accounted for so they sit just above ground level, fanned out at increasing distances with slight lateral scatter and occasional stacking. I'm also planning standing goblets placed upright near the chest and coin piles, working out their floor positions in a top-down layout of the scene.

I'm simplifying the coordinate system by keeping the chest centered at the origin in z, defining the front spill pile as a flattened hemisphere positioned just in front of the chest where it meets and slightly overlaps the chest's front wall.

I'm checking that the pile's height near the lock plate stays low enough to keep the lock mostly visible, so I'm shifting the pile's center off to the side to clear that area.

For the left pile, I'm placing a hemisphere mound with a goblet standing upright on top, its foot slightly embedded into the coin surface for a settled look. The right pile gets a smaller hemisphere with its own goblet positioned similarly, and I'm figuring out where to rest the crown on the front pile as well.

Checking the geometry, I'm adjusting the front pile's center position so the crown sits closer to the peak rather than on a steep slope -- recalculating the height ratio puts it near y≈0.19 with a slight forward tilt so the rim naturally sinks into the coins on one side.

I realize coins scattered across the pile could poke through the crown's mesh or sit visibly under the red cap dome where they shouldn't be seen. I'm adding a filter to the coin scatter that excludes any coin positions within a small radius of the crown's center, so the area directly beneath the crown stays clear and only the mound's base surface shows through.

For the hextech crystal clusters, I'm positioning two groups behind the chest—one at the right-back and one at the left-back—each made of tilted cyan hexagonal prisms with pointed cone tips, glowing and varying in height and angle, staying under the overall scene height limit.

Instead of floating sparkle cards above the hoard, which would break the "nothing hangs above it" rule, I'll place small star-glint cards directly on the gems and coins themselves, oriented along their surface normals so they read as glints rather than hovering elements.

For the chest decals, I'll make a textured gold scroll ornament plane placed just in front of the body wall, facing forward with diamond/scroll/rivet motifs in light gold stroke and dark outline, and extend similar ornamentation to the side panels.

Now I'm working out the lid's emblem decal — projecting it onto the curved arch top using an explicit bone binding so it stays rigid with the lid, choosing an upward orientation so the design reads correctly once the lid is opened and the top faces backward.

I'm also setting up the interior lining decal: a crest plane positioned just under the lid's apex, facing downward, and working out its rotation axis so the emblem orients correctly once the lid swings open roughly 105 degrees.

Checking the local axis frame confirms it's consistent and reads correctly from the facing side with no mirroring issue. For the chest, I'll add small gold ball feet and a gold base plinth strip at the bottom, then start adding scattered treasure extras around it.

Since the subject list only mentions coins, gems, chest, crown, and goblets, I'll skip gold bars but add a couple of neat coin stacks near the chest using slightly offset, rotated cylinders—one taller stack and one shorter one, plus a leaning coin for realism. I'm also considering adding a draped pearl necklace using a curved sweep from the chest.

For the necklace, I'll drape it over the front pile by defining a rough path and using a surface-drape function that pulls each sample point onto the nearest surface, lifting it slightly so it sits above the coins rather than sinking into them.

Coins scattered on the pile might sink under or poke through the necklace beads given the lift and tilt values, but that's probably an acceptable visual tradeoff. I also need to double check the sweep API usage, since draping returns a path that gets fed into the sweep function with a radius and bone reference.

Now I'm sketching out the actual module structure, being careful to avoid unused variables and untyped `any` since type-checking seems strict. I'm starting with the imports needed from the builder library and its clockwork and glow kits.

Writing import statements...

For the paint palette, I'm defining a gold metal paint for chest bands and crown elements, and considering a custom stylized gold paint with a warm gradient ramp from bright yellow at the top to darker shadow tones, aiming for a painted League-of-Legends aesthetic rather than flat metallic shading.

Writing the hand() paint helper...

Writing wood paint logic...

Working out plank seam logic...

Then I'll add a highlight line next to each seam for depth, define a red velvet lining paint with layered noise, and set flat gold-tone tints for the coins. I'm leaning toward a cutGem helper using lathe geometry to generate faceted gem shapes efficiently.

Defining gem profile points...

I'm thinking about varying gem shapes for diversity — lathe-cut rounds, octahedron diamonds, dodecahedron cabochons — each placed on piles with random tilt via a gemOn helper, using flat-colored glow materials cloned per color so the gems get that faceted, slightly emissive look without full brightness.

Working through the gold trim bands on the lid, placing them near x=±0.29-0.31 with end caps as full gold plates to match the chest body's banding style.

Still thinking through the velvet cap stripes, goblet gem bands, and chest wood planks as paint-based textures rather than geometry, plus deciding on two coin face variants (crown and skull/gem) alongside a side medallion, crest, and sparkle texture to keep the total texture count around five or six.

I'm now adding a quilted diamond pattern texture for the lid lining, colored red with gold button dots, applied to the lining box so it shows on the underside and faces while keeping the crest as a separate overlay plane.

I'm estimating coin counts for the piles, aiming for roughly 240 overlapping coins across the scatter areas so coverage looks dense without blowing past a reasonable triangle budget—landing around 10k triangles and 450 parts total.
